title: Emergency volumes: IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL by age band, buccal and IV anticonvulsants
blurb: Turn adrenaline micrograms into mL from a 1 mg/mL ampoule, and calculate buccal and intravenous anticonvulsant volumes from the strength given.
question: A child aged 9 years with anaphylaxis is prescribed adrenaline 300 micrograms by intramuscular injection. The ampoule is labelled 1 mg in 1 mL (1 in 1,000). What volume should be drawn up?

teach.body: Formal rule: adrenaline 1 in 1,000 contains 1 mg in 1 mL, which is 1000 micrograms in 1 mL, so volume (mL) = dose in micrograms ÷ 1000. Plain English: every 100 micrograms is 0.1 mL. Emergency items are stretch questions on Part A, but the arithmetic is the same want ÷ have, with a micrograms to mg step first.

teach.caption: Resuscitation Council UK 2021. In the exam the prescribed dose is always given.

teach.h: Worked example: Ruby on a children's ward
teach.body: Ruby Clarke, 9, develops anaphylaxis on a children's ward after eating peanuts. Adrenaline 300 micrograms IM is prescribed, and the ampoule is 1 mg in 1 mL (1 in 1,000). Convert: 300 micrograms = 0.3 mg. Volume = 0.3 ÷ 1 × 1 = 0.3 mL. Sense-check: 1 mL holds 1000 micrograms, so 300 micrograms is three tenths of a mL.

teach.caption: IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis uses the 1 in 1,000 (1 mg/mL) strength.

teach.text: 1 in 1,000 is 1 mg/mL; 1 in 10,000 is ten times weaker (0.1 mg/mL). Using the wrong strength gives a tenfold volume error. Also watch the micrograms to mg step: 300 micrograms is 0.3 mg, not 3 mg or 0.03 mg.

teach.h: Buccal midazolam: read the strength every time
teach.body: Buccal midazolam comes in more than one strength (for example 5 mg in 1 mL and 10 mg in 1 mL), so the same 10 mg dose can be 2 mL or 1 mL. Use the strength printed in the question or on the person's own prefilled syringe. Intravenous anticonvulsants such as lorazepam and phenytoin follow the same want ÷ have × volume rule.

summary: You can now convert emergency adrenaline doses in micrograms to mL from a 1 in 1,000 ampoule and recall the RCUK age bands for context. You can also calculate buccal and intravenous anticonvulsant volumes from the strength given, including a capped dose.

A.q: A child aged 9 years with anaphylaxis is prescribed adrenaline 300 micrograms by intramuscular injection. The ampoule is labelled 1 mg in 1 mL (1 in 1,000). What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: This uses 100 micrograms per mL, the 1 in 10,000 strength.
whyNot.2: This converts 300 micrograms to 0.03 mg, a tenfold error.
whyNot.3: This divides micrograms by a mg label without converting.

A.q: A baby aged 4 months with anaphylaxis is prescribed adrenaline 100 micrograms by intramuscular injection. The ampoule is labelled 1 mg in 1 mL (1 in 1,000). What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: This uses 100 micrograms per mL, the 1 in 10,000 strength.
whyNot.1: This converts 100 micrograms to 0.01 mg, a tenfold error.
whyNot.2: This is the volume for 150 micrograms; the prescription is 100.

A.q: A client aged 8 years is prescribed buccal midazolam 7.5 mg for a prolonged seizure. The oromucosal solution label reads 5 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: This uses a 10 mg in 1 mL strength, not the 5 mg in 1 mL on the label (0.75 rounds to 0.8).
whyNot.2: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.
whyNot.3: This drops the decimal point in 7.5 mg, a tenfold error.

B.q: A child aged 4 years with anaphylaxis is prescribed adrenaline 150 micrograms by intramuscular injection. The ampoule is labelled 1 mg in 1 mL (1 in 1,000). What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: This uses 100 micrograms per mL, the 1 in 10,000 strength.
whyNot.1: This converts 150 micrograms to 0.015 mg, a tenfold error.
whyNot.3: This rounds to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

B.q: A child is prescribed buccal midazolam 5 mg for a prolonged seizure. The prefilled oral syringe label reads 10 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: This uses a 5 mg in 1 mL strength, not the 10 mg in 1 mL on the label.
whyNot.2: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.
whyNot.3: This reads the label as 100 mg in 1 mL, a tenfold error.

B.q: A client weighing 48 kg is prescribed lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg to a maximum of 4 mg by intravenous injection for a prolonged seizure. The ampoule label reads 4 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.
B.why: 0.1 × 48 = 4.8 mg, which is above the 4 mg maximum, so the dose is 4 mg. Volume = 4 ÷ 4 × 1 = 1 mL.

whyNot.0: This gives 4.8 mg and misses the 4 mg maximum.
whyNot.1: This writes the 4 mg dose as 4 mL.
whyNot.2: This divides the label strength by the uncapped dose, an inverted sum.

C.q: An adult with anaphylaxis is given adrenaline 500 micrograms by intramuscular injection, and the same dose is repeated once after 5 minutes. What total dose of adrenaline has been given in mg? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.1: This counts only one of the two doses.
whyNot.2: This gives the micrograms total but labels it mg.
whyNot.3: This divides by 10,000, a tenfold error.

C.q: An ampoule labelled adrenaline 1 in 1,000 contains 1 mg in 1 mL. A second ampoule is labelled 1 in 10,000, which is 1 mg in 10 mL. What volume of the 1 in 10,000 solution contains the same amount of adrenaline as 0.5 mL of the 1 in 1,000 solution? Please use the correct unit.
C.why: 0.5 mL of 1 in 1,000 holds 0.5 mg. 1 in 10,000 holds 0.1 mg per mL, so 0.5 ÷ 0.1 = 5 mL.

whyNot.0: This divides by 10 instead of multiplying: the weaker solution needs more volume.
whyNot.1: This assumes both strengths are the same.
whyNot.3: This treats 1 in 10,000 as one hundred times weaker.

C.q: A client weighing 48 kg is prescribed a phenytoin loading dose of 20 mg/kg by intravenous infusion for status epilepticus. The vial label reads phenytoin 250 mg in 5 mL. What volume of phenytoin should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
C.why: Dose = 20 × 48 = 960 mg. Volume = 960 ÷ 250 × 5 = 19.2 mL. Sense-check: 250 mg in 5 mL is 50 mg per mL, and 960 ÷ 50 = 19.2.

whyNot.0: This forgets the 5 mL stock volume (3.84 rounds to 3.8).
whyNot.2: This is have ÷ want (250 ÷ 960 × 5), the inverted fraction.
whyNot.3: This treats the label as 250 mg in 10 mL, doubling the volume.

reteach.title: 100 micrograms = 0.1 mL
reteach.question: How do you turn an adrenaline dose in micrograms into mL from a 1 mg in 1 mL ampoule?

blocks.body: 1 mg/mL is 1000 micrograms in each mL. Divide the micrograms by 1000: 500 → 0.5 mL, 300 → 0.3 mL, 150 → 0.15 mL.

blocks.text: Using 100 micrograms per mL (the 1 in 10,000 strength) makes every volume ten times too big.

explain.body: 1 in 1,000 = 1 g in 1,000 mL = 1 mg in 1 mL. 1 mg = 1000 micrograms.

test.q: Adrenaline 1 in 1,000 contains 1 mg in 1 mL. How many micrograms of adrenaline are in 1 mL?
test.why: 1 mg = 1000 micrograms, so 1 mL contains 1000 micrograms.

whyNot.0: This is the strength of 1 in 10,000, not 1 in 1,000.
whyNot.1: This converts mg to micrograms by × 10.
whyNot.2: This keeps the number in mg but labels it micrograms.

test.q: An adult with anaphylaxis is prescribed adrenaline 500 micrograms by intramuscular injection. The ampoule is labelled 1 mg in 1 mL (1 in 1,000). What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.1: This uses 100 micrograms per mL, the 1 in 10,000 strength.
whyNot.2: This converts 500 micrograms to 0.05 mg, a tenfold error.
whyNot.3: This divides by 10, a hundredfold error.

explain.body: Multiply mL by 1000 to get micrograms at 1 mg/mL. 0.15 mL × 1000 = 150 micrograms.
